articles.title: Germany target of 'intensive' espionage, Merz says after suspected Russian spy arrest
articles.summary: A Ukrainian man was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia - one of several such cases in Germany this year.
body: Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Russian intelligence activity in Germany remains 'at a consistently high level'
Germany is the target of "intensive" espionage activity, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said after a Ukrainian national was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia.
Officials said the suspect, named as Vadym Y., had allegedly collected military-related intelligence from Germany.
Merz called the uncovering of the case a "success", but warned "let us not delude ourselves - the activities of Russian intelligence services in Germany remain at a consistently high level".

Several people alleged to be acting on behalf of Russia and other foreign powers have been arrested in Germany this year. Germany has been one of the leading European suppliers of weapons to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

The German Federal Prosecutor General's Office said on Thursday that Vadym Y., as he was identified under German privacy law, had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025.
It also said the Ukrainian man had collected information including "on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition, and explosives".
He is due to appear before an investigating judge on Friday.
In January, a woman was arrested in Berlin suspected of gathering information for an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy.
Other arrests this year included a Romanian woman and a Ukrainian man accused of spying on an individual supplying drones from Germany to Ukraine, according to the prosecutor's office.
UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham in Berlin
Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid

And, the former German spy chief August Hanning was arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power earlier this month. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.
Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.
Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D and accused him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents in exchange for money.
Speaking at the sidelines of a conference in Montenegro on Thursday, Merz said: "We will likely see more such cases in the coming months and years."
Merz reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier this month, including tackling hybrid attacks and hostile activity.
The talks between the two leaders came after Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport in September.
Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Russia.

articles.title: At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
articles.summary: The deaths include two women found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.
body: A car lies abandoned after severe rainfall in Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts, near Marseille
At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam.
The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport.
The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.

Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead. Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death.

In the towns of Mouriès and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area.
Roads and train lines ‌in ⁠the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post ​on X.
"The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-Rhône department, said in a statement on Wednesday.
Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues."
A local resident shows her house which has been flooded following severe rainfall in Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts, near Marseille
More severe weather is forecast in France, with Storm Austen - a newly named weather system moving in from the Atlantic - expected to reach the country's north-west.
France's weather service, Météo-France, has issued an orange-level wind warning for five western departments from Thursday evening into Friday.
The alert covers Côtes-d'Armor, Finistère, Morbihan, Ille-et-Vilaine and Manche.
Heavy rainfall that began on 19 October caused significant flooding in south-eastern France
Storm Adam had already brought severe flooding to eastern Spain, where at least three people were killed.
Several towns along the Mediterranean coast were cut off by floodwaters, while helicopters were deployed to rescue people stranded on rooftops.
Members of the Military Emergencies Unit found the body of a woman in the town of Oliva, Valencia, during rescue operations on Monday.

Two other women were confirmed dead over ⁠the weekend. One woman's body was washed up on a beach in Sagunto, in the eastern region of Valencia, and another was swept away by floodwaters in Cabrera de Mar, near Barcelona.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez made a promise that the national government would provide resources to help in reconstruction during a visit to the Valencia region on Tuesday.
The Valencian government approved on Tuesday an aid package of €23.5m (£20m) for those affected by Storm Adam.

articles.title: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
articles.summary: The Brazilian president accuses the tech firm of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro, which it denies.
body: Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro in the second round of voting on Sunday

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.

In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.
In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.
The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.
It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.
A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.

It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts".
"Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read.
Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally.
Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted.
Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula.
Pro-Lula supporters gathered outside Meta's office in São Paulo on Monday, accusing the company of interference in the Brazilian electoral process
Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office.
Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.

On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network".
The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election.
Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power".
He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes.
Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.

articles.title: Total ban on protests in Marseille and Lyon after riots
articles.summary: Protests will only be allowed in some towns and cities if organised by unions, and top museums will be closed on Saturday.
body: The tourism office in Lyon was set on fire during protests last weekend, the city has banned all demonstrations this Saturday
France will impose a total ban on protests in the country's second and third largest cities, Marseille and Lyon, this weekend.
In the parts of the country where protests are not banned completely, only authorised union protests will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said.
The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in Paris will also be closed on Saturday as more protests are expected in the city.
Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.
France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.
Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.
Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper.
Public transport Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city.
The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses.

The prefecture for the Rhône region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT).
Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.
Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.

"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced.
"When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.

Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Unrest spread across several French cities last weekend, including the capital Paris
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.

Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

articles.title: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother
articles.summary: Her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy is airing the ad featuring her mother, whose husband was charged with sexual abuse in her childhood.
body: Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable".
Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday evening, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done".

In the ad Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody.
Since it launched on Monday, the ad has generated political backlash and cast a national spotlight on the race.
Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election.
In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down.
"I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening.
"You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad.
According to information provided to the BBC by Acton's campaign, the last time she saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted.
Arthur's husband fled town before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted, and died in 2004.
In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point".

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it.
Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state.
The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet The Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling".
On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor.
"And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."
MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election.
Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about controversial Ohio attack ad
President Donald Trump has said: "It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much.
"But I don't think that has anything to do with Vivek."
Meanwhile, Vice-President JD Vance has said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.
David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that attack ads are not new in US politics but said "they have become more intense".
He suggested Ramaswamy's ad could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour.
A poll by VoteHub, external released on Thursday suggested Acton was leading Ramaswamy by 1%, within the margin of error, and noted the surveys were done before the ad.
If Acton wins, she would be the first Democrat elected as Ohio governor in two decades.

articles.title: Meta strikes deal to stop Mark Zuckerberg leaving California over billionaire tax
articles.summary: The Meta boss had said he would exit the state over a wealth tax that has not yet come into force.
body: Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg
Meta has agreed a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to stop the Facebook co-founder from leaving California after he threatened to move from the state because of a proposed tax on billionaires.
The agreement allows Zuckerberg - reportedly one of the world's richest people - to sell shares in Meta without losing control of the Californian-based company if he needs to pay a large tax bill.
The measure, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on state residents with a net worth of more than $1bn (£750m), is yet to pass. Californian residents will vote on 3 November.
Nevertheless, Zuckerberg secured a deal with a special committee at Meta after "robust", and "at several points, contentious" negotiations.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
Zuckerberg - who has a $226bn fortune according to Forbes' billionaires tracker - had told Meta's board that it was his intention to remain with the firm for "the foreseeable future".

However, he said he was evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and, if he listed his home on the real estate market, it "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees".
This, he told the board, "would raise questions for management of the company going forward".

A special committee within Meta decided it was "critically important" to keep Zuckerberg in a leadership role and in California to manage the firm from its headquarters "during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry".
Tech companies in the US and globally are spending billions of dollars on developing artificial intelligence and the infrastructure around it.
Meta said the share deal was appropriate to ensure Zuckerberg "remains working closely" with the company's AI at its headquarters.
It said his "talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the special committee wants that to continue".

articles.title: 'Looksmaxxing' influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge
articles.summary: The influencer, whose real name is Braden Peters, is accused of sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl in 2025.
body: Clavicular, a social media influencer who promotes the "looksmaxxing" trend of young men maximising their attractiveness, has pleaded not guilty to criminal charges including rape.
The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Peters, was charged in September with felony rape, drugging an individual for sexual intercourse and procuring alcohol for someone under the age of 21.
The charges stem from an incident in 2025 when he is accused of assaulting a 17-year-old girl at his family's Massachusetts home.
Peters has denied the allegations and said the encounter was consensual. On Thursday, he was granted $10,000 bail, ordered not to contact or post about his accuser, and to surrender his passport.
Clavicular walks a runway at Paris Fashion Week in June 2026

A woman told police that on 23 May 2025, Peters ordered her an Uber to his family's house in Chatham where they were drinking alcohol while filming a livestream before he allegedly raped her, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
The police officer who took the report said he believed she was unable to consent due to her age and the level of intoxication she exhibited in the livestream, CBS reported.
Clavicular has more than a million followers on TikTok and Instagram and has garnered media attention for extreme measures he has taken for "looksmaxxing".

He has admitted to using a hammer on his face and jawline and taking a number of steroids, injections, and other drugs to achieve bodily perfection. He also gives advice on appearing masculine and performs stunts to shock followers.
In Florida earlier this year, he was charged after filming himself shooting at what appeared to be a dead alligator. He pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public.
In March, he was arrested on suspicion of battery after authorities suspected him of instigating a fight between two women. Authorities said in July that they did not intend to file charges.
After Thursday's hearing, Peters posted a photo of himself in the black suit and black tie he wore to court, while holding his dog which he also brought to court.
His next hearing will be on 24 November, when the judge will decide if there is enough evidence for the case to move forward.

articles.title: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
articles.summary: Officials compare working in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine to the Cold War era.
body: Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre Lévy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow
"Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.
US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.

But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.
The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.

They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts, and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.

Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.

Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.
"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."
The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.
Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023
Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.
"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.

Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.
The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".

Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.
One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.
Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back

Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police.
One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear.
Not everyone can deal with the pressure.
One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months.
In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre Lévy.
He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be.

The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible.
And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies.
Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country.
But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning.
Pierre Lévy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024

After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Еven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers.
One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'."

Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses.

A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase.
"It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour."
A wooden replica of the Great Seal of the US was given to the American ambassador to Russia as a gift in 1945 - it was later found to contain a listening device
Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".

Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.

This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."
Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."
But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow.
"Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."
Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.
But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians.
"Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."
